hook.first_sentence: You downloaded a twenty-seven billion parameter model and it would not fit.

scenes.narration: You downloaded a twenty-seven billion parameter model and it would not fit. The original file, in BF16, the model's full-precision format, weighs about fifty-three gigabytes. Your gaming card holds twelve gigabytes, so the download stops at the loading bar.

What changed is a single file called NariQ. It repacks Qwen three point eight twenty-seven B, the Qwen model with twenty-seven billion parameters. The squeeze is quantization, storing every number in the model with fewer bits. The download is ten point one two gigabytes. It arrives as one GGUF, the single file format your local tools already speak.

scenes.narration: BF16, the model's full sixteen-bit memory, spends sixteen bits on every number. NariQ spends three. Fewer bits per number means a smaller file. The old fear said anything under four bits wrecks the model. That fear had evidence behind it, until this file.

DeepSWE, a benchmark where an AI agent completes real software tasks, is the long test. The three-bit file scored forty-one. The full original scored thirty-nine point eight. The honest catch: Nari Labs graded its own homework. Both scores come from Nari Labs' modified copy of llama.cpp, the engine most local tools use.

Sixteen bits became three, and the file shrank to about a fifth of itself. That is how a twelve-gigabyte card becomes a candidate. Think of it like rounding pi down to three point one. The loss is real and uneven: exact long math notices it first, casual chat never does.

Now the fine print that protects you. The file runs only through Nari Labs' modified llama.cpp, slower than ordinary compressed models except on one workstation card. Stock llama.cpp, Ollama, and LM Studio cannot load it yet. GeForce cards have not been tested yet. Any speed promise you hear tonight is folklore.
What this file earns is a narrow title: good enough for agent work on your card. Not as good as BF16 everywhere. For exact long math, BF16 stays the choice.

The numbers say a twenty-seven billion parameter model now fits inside a gaming card. The question was never whether the model was smart enough for your card. The wall was never intelligence; it was memory.
